title: REG U4·W4 — Business Law II: Debtor-Creditor, Secured Transactions, Bankruptcy & Securities
lessonHtml:
Cold open — what happens when debts go bad

A contractor lives on credit — supplier accounts, equipment loans, surety bonds — so the law of debtor and creditor matters as much as tax. This final REG week covers suretyship, the UCC Article 9 rules that govern secured transactions, the bankruptcy process when a debtor cannot pay, and the federal securities laws that regulate raising capital. These are the rules that decide who gets paid, in what order, when money runs short.

Suretyship

A surety promises a creditor to answer for the debt of another (the principal debtor) — the construction performance and payment bonds a contractor posts are suretyship arrangements. A surety is primarily liable (the creditor can pursue it directly), whereas a guarantor is typically secondarily liable. A surety who pays gains powerful rights: subrogation (stepping into the creditor's position), reimbursement from the debtor, and contribution from co-sureties. Key surety defenses include fraud on the surety and a material modification of the underlying contract without consent — though the debtor's personal defenses (like incapacity) generally do not protect the surety.

Secured transactions — attachment

UCC Article 9 governs a security interest in personal property and fixtures. The interest first attaches — becoming enforceable against the debtor — when three things exist: (1) value is given by the creditor, (2) the debtor has rights in the collateral, and (3) there is a security agreement (authenticated/signed describing the collateral) or the creditor takes possession or control. Attachment is what makes the lender a secured party as between it and the borrower — but not yet against the rest of the world.

Secured transactions — perfection and priority

Perfection makes the security interest effective against third parties, usually by filing a financing statement (debtor name, secured party, collateral) in the public records, or by possession, by control (for deposit accounts/investment property), or automatically for a purchase-money security interest in consumer goods. Priority rules then rank competing claims: a perfected interest beats an unperfected one; between two perfected interests, the first to file or perfect wins; and a purchase-money security interest (PMSI) in inventory or equipment can take superpriority if its special timing and notice requirements are met. On default, the secured party may repossess and dispose of the collateral in a commercially reasonable manner.

Bankruptcy — the basics and the chapters

Federal bankruptcy gives an honest debtor a fresh start and an orderly creditor payout. Chapter 7 is liquidation — a trustee sells nonexempt assets and distributes the proceeds. Chapter 11 is business reorganization under a court-approved plan. Chapter 13 is an individual's adjustment of debts from future income. Filing triggers the automatic stay, which immediately halts collection efforts, lawsuits, and foreclosures — giving the estate breathing room and protecting the orderly process.

Bankruptcy — the estate, preferences, and priority

The trustee can avoid certain pre-bankruptcy transfers. A voidable preference is a payment to a creditor on an antecedent debt made while insolvent within 90 days before filing (or one year for an insider) that lets that creditor receive more than it would in liquidation — the trustee claws it back for equal treatment. Fraudulent transfers can be unwound too. Distribution follows a strict order: secured creditors are paid from their collateral first, then priority unsecured claims (administrative expenses, certain employee wages up to a cap, and certain taxes), then general unsecured creditors pro rata. The debtor receives a discharge of most remaining debts — but some debts (recent taxes, most student loans, alimony/child support, debts from fraud) are nondischargeable.

Federal securities — the 1933 Act

The Securities Act of 1933 regulates the initial issuance of securities: a public offering must be registered with the SEC and accompanied by a prospectus full disclosure, unless an exemption applies. Common exemptions include Regulation D private placements (notably Rule 506, allowing unlimited capital from accredited investors), intrastate offerings, and small offerings. Liability under the 1933 Act attaches for material misstatements or omissions in the registration statement — a near-strict-liability standard for the issuer, with a due-diligence defense available to others.

Federal securities — the 1934 Act

The Securities Exchange Act of 1934 governs ongoing trading and reporting (the 10-K/10-Q/8-K filings from BAR Unit 2). Its antifraud core, §10(b) and Rule 10b-5, prohibits fraud or material misstatements in connection with the purchase or sale of any security — the basis for most insider-trading cases, which require scienter (intent). §16(b) forces insiders (officers, directors, >10% owners) to disgorge short-swing profits on purchases and sales within six months. Together the two Acts protect investors at issuance and in the secondary market, completing the legal framework REG tests.

Other creditor remedies and consumer protections

Beyond Article 9, creditors have remedies and limits. An unsecured creditor who obtains a judgment can enforce it through a writ of execution against property, a garnishment of wages (capped by federal law to protect a portion of earnings), or a judgment lien on real estate. Construction creditors have a special tool — the mechanic's lien — securing payment for labor and materials supplied to improve real property, and a fixture filing lets a secured party claim goods that become attached to real estate. On the protective side, federal consumer statutes — the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, the Truth in Lending Act, and the Fair Credit Reporting Act — regulate how debts are collected, disclosed, and reported, and certain debtor property (a homestead, tools of the trade, basic personal items) is exempt from creditors. A creditor's choice among these remedies turns on what the debtor owns and which liens have already attached, so the secured, judgment, and statutory tools are weighed together. These rules shape the practical contest between a creditor trying to collect and a debtor trying to survive.

CMA bridge

MBG's equipment lenders file Article 9 financing statements to perfect their liens; its surety backs the performance bonds on public jobs; and if a major customer files bankruptcy, the preference and priority rules decide whether MBG keeps payments it already received. The CFO who tracks lien positions and bond obligations is applying exactly this body of law to protect the company's cash.

Practice and recap

  1. Distinguish a surety (primarily liable) from a guarantor; identify subrogation, reimbursement, and contribution rights and surety defenses.
  2. Apply Article 9: attachment (value + debtor rights + security agreement/possession), perfection (file/possess/control/automatic PMSI), priority (perfected > unperfected; first to file/perfect; PMSI superpriority).
  3. Compare bankruptcy Chapters 7/11/13, the automatic stay, voidable preferences (90 days / 1 year insiders), the priority waterfall, and nondischargeable debts.
  4. Apply the 1933 Act (registration + Reg D/Rule 506 exemptions) and the 1934 Act (§10(b)/Rule 10b-5 fraud, §16(b) short-swing profits).

Recap: a surety is primarily liable with rights of subrogation, reimbursement, and contribution; an Article 9 security interest attaches with value, debtor rights, and a security agreement, then perfects by filing/possession/control (or automatically for a consumer-goods PMSI), with priority to the first to file or perfect and superpriority for a PMSI; bankruptcy halts collection via the automatic stay, lets the trustee avoid preferences (90 days, or 1 year for insiders), and pays secured then priority then general unsecured creditors before discharging dischargeable debts; and the 1933 Act governs registration of new offerings (with Reg D exemptions) while the 1934 Act polices trading through Rule 10b-5 and §16(b).

Effective against third parties by filing a financing statement, possession, control, or automatically for a PMSI in consumer goods.

questions.q: A security interest attaches when value is given, the debtor has rights in the collateral, and:
choices: There is a security agreement (or the creditor has possession/control)
questions.explain: Attachment requires value, debtor rights, and a security agreement (or possession/control). Filing is for perfection, not attachment.

questions.q: Between two perfected security interests in the same collateral, priority goes to:
choices: The first to file or perfect
questions.explain: Among perfected interests, the first to file or perfect has priority (with PMSI superpriority exceptions).

questions.q: A payment to an ordinary creditor on an old debt, made while insolvent 60 days before filing, may be:
choices: A voidable preference clawed back by the trustee
questions.explain: Preferential transfers within 90 days (1 year for insiders) can be avoided by the trustee.

questions.q: Which bankruptcy chapter is a business reorganization?
questions.explain: Chapter 11 is reorganization; Chapter 7 is liquidation; Chapter 13 is individual debt adjustment.

questions.q: Rule 506 of Regulation D allows an issuer to raise capital primarily from:
questions.explain: Rule 506 permits unlimited capital from accredited investors (with limits on non-accredited investors).

questions.q: Section 16(b) of the 1934 Act requires insiders to disgorge:
choices: Short-swing profits on trades within six months
questions.explain: §16(b) recovers short-swing profits from purchases and sales within a six-month period by insiders.

questions.q: A surety who pays the creditor is entitled to:
choices: Subrogation and reimbursement from the debtor
questions.explain: A paying surety steps into the creditor's rights (subrogation) and may seek reimbursement from the debtor and contribution from co-sureties.
